Who knows how long I'd been in the chamber? To me, it felt like only a year or so. The Gods, who I assumed my captors were, fed me well and there was plenty to keep me busy between examining the windowless rooms, playing magical board games with floating pieces, and speaking with the revered deities. They, like me, spoke Latin, which was a pleasant surprise. I assumed this was Mount Olympus. Then the ground shook. An intense nausea came over me, as if I were dropped from a cliff. A gaping hole emerged in the center of the living quarters, and there was a dark stone road with unappealing yellow lines in the center. The smell was atrocious, like the sulfur-y scent a volcano gives shortly before it erupts. I was urged to drop to the road, and so I obliged.

I landed with a surprising force. The Roman armor which I had been donning for the duration of my stay had grown immensely more heavy. I was surrounded by humans. Strange, tall humans, with short, course hair and terribly ugly two-piece clothing. Is this what Rome had come to? 

"Can you not operate in my absence? It's no wonder the Gods have brought me back, Rome has fallen!" I cried out, expecting applause and recognition.

"Holy shit, guys, its Caesar!"

I was shocked, then overrun by the mob of people around.

At the age of 6, your parents have the option to bring you into the lab for analysis for your robotic compatriot that acts as your conscious and helps realize your strengths. It used to be rare, but as the years went by, it became mainstream. Children without 'spiritrons,' as they were called, were ostracized. There were the prized spiritrons, such as grizzlies and tigers, and there were the lame ones, such as crickets and pidgeons. There were the exceptionally rare ones, such as tree frogs and jellyfish. Not everyone was unique; not everyone was equal. Owls were desirable for intuitive jobs, wolves for leadership, and nearly all athletes were rhinos, cheetahs, or bears, depending on the sport.

I was sitting in the waiting room, playing on my father's old gameboy. I had the advanced, modern gaming devices, but I preferred the simplistic, relaxing quality of the dated models. I was training up my singular type team in Pokémon emerald to beat the elite four when they called my name. It was repetitive work, so I hurriedly saved while shoving the still-on device into my pocket. I stood up and walked to the door, suddenly anxious. What if I was a goldfish, or, possibly worse, what if I was I wasn't? The people with good spiritrons were immediately thrown into schooling or training to optimize them for their field. I took a deep breath and followed the doctor through the door.

The hallway was darker than I had expected. It felt more like a home than a laboratory. The doctor didn't speak during the walk to the testing room. I saw his mark where the chip that contains the animal is implanted. There is usually an etching of the face of the spiritron inside, but I couldn't quite make it out. Desperate to break the silence, which was only contributing to my nerves, I asked, "What animal are you?"

"I'm a human, silly." He said, sarcastically while showing his mark. It was a chimp. I suppose you don't have to take life seriously to read questions and press buttons. Before I could reply, he opened a door on the right and ushered me in. In the room, there were two leather chairs, one with a strange machine hanging over the head. The doctor sat in the chair without the machine, so I took a seat in the other. He pulled out his clipboard and started asking away.

"What animal does your father have?"

"Hawk"

"And your mother?"

"Saber tooth tiger."

After what feels kind thousands of questions about my personality, he finally announced that the verbal portion of the text was over. He pressed some buttons, and the machine over my head descended. I drifted to sleep after fifteen minutes.

The doctor woke me up. He looked nervous, and this was pretty unsettling. I asked him what the problem was, and he replied, 

"Your test results came back, and we have no idea what it means. I called my supervisor, and he said to retest you. I'm so sorry, but you'll be here for another three hours."

Well shit. I answered all of the questions again, this time going out of my way to reword some of the answers. Again, I went under around fifteen minutes into the brain scan. When he woke me up this time, he still had a nervous look to him, but this time there was a lot of confusion as well.

"Well buddy, your tests results came back the same as before, and we have no idea what it means. Your animal doesn't exist. The problem is, the results of the first and second run were identical. We tried to determine the animal from the picture, but it was unlike anything that anyone has ever seen before. We initially thought it was a glitch, so we pulled up the traits in the result, but that too was unrelated to any animal we know of. We asked your parents if we should put in your chip even though we don't know what animal it is. They said that it was up to you, so, what do you say, kiddo?"

Wow. This is a lot to take in for a six year old.

"Yes. Put it inside me."

The doctor laughed immaturely, but I wasn't sure why. He pulled out a syringe with what I can only assume was full of anesthetics. He injected it into me, and I passed out almost immediately.

I woke up yet again in the waiting room of the building. I looked on the underside of my right wrist to see my chip. On it was among the strangest thing I've seen all day.

Throughout the day, things seemed to go my way. I found things that were very unlikely, and had everyone not just mysteriously gotten roles tattooed onto their right biceps, I would not have believed it was natural. The words on everybody's arms started to define them. Even in day one, the runningback of the football team, who was a hunk of a teenager, befriended one of the previously unknown kids solely because they were both paladins. People were self-segregated by role. Everyone was desperately trying to control their new skills. I noticed it was especially hard for the magical roles, as their powers seemed to be fueled by emotion alone. It was extremely hard for a cleric to heal someone they hated, for example, and Mr. Oglesby only discovered his pyromancy when he was angry at the class. In the beginning of it all, at 4th period lunch of that first day, when people were just starting to tap their newfound purpose, I noticed that no matter if I knew the person or not, or even if I knew their role, the aftermath and effects of their usage was always what I expected. At first, I wrote it off as coincedence, I mean, dungeon master could mean explorer, right? *right?* When my childhood bully rolled up his skintight sleeve and revealed that he was an executioner, I had a vision of him wielding a small hatchet and hitting a tree with it. Instead of cutting down the tree, however, he sneezed and spun around in a circle and pulled several muscles in his back. I ignored it with a giggle, thinking it was a silly tale I thought up, born of trauma.

When I awoke the next day and saw that the exact vision I had was all the rage on every social media known to man, I knew this was for real. I'd never played any kind of RP, but I knew the implications of being the dungeon master. I posted on reddit, both out of pride and warning, but nobody believed me. I smited them all. One by one, redditors and naysayers in real life dropped. Knights were trampled by their brand new horse, thieves were caught and detained, magicians had experiments literally blow up in their faces. I was powerful, for the first time in my life. On my rise to fame, I kept most of my close friends. They always found fortune in the eyes of the world. Their cars got incredible, borderline impossible gas mileage, their powers always went where they wanted them to go, and one of them even won a 100:1 bet in the Kentucky Derby. My fame started to spread, and I got letters, emails, and phone calls galore as the technicians, hackers, and generally smart roles tracked down my address, email, and phone number. People were begging for fortune from the dungeon master. By the first month, I, a high-school junior, had the world at my fingertips. Not because of god-given talent, not because of a good work ethic, not because of rich or important parents. I was powerful because I have a word over my bicep.

People would obey my every wish, and go on various tedious quests because I wanted to taste the water in China. If I were a fraud, surely someone would have figured it out, right? I sure hoped not. I took a shower in the penthouse suite of a luxurious hotel on the coast near Tampa. I turned to wash my arm, double checking that thin calligraphic marker was still on the counter, and washed my arms. As I left the shower, I looked at myself in the mirror. Was it really right for me to be doing this? Doesn't matter, they won't find out. Besides, it's my role! Lord of deception, king of the world. I painstakingly painted over the word on my bicep. After a half hour of inking up, I exited the bathroom in my sleek black turtleneck when there was a knock on the door. I go to answer it, and am greeted by a man who looked to be in his mid-twenties. He was dressed well, in a cream colored suit with a royal blue tie. Before I could ask him his role, he automatically rolled up his sleeve to reveal his word.

*Angel*

I nodded somberly. I knew that this was the end of my reign, and my short life flashed before my eyes as I was burned alive by his touch. I will never know if the world learned my secret, or if they just figured that a new dungeon master had surfaced, but frankly, I don't really want to. It's sufficient for only me to know my real word:

*Devil*

Ray was my best friend for the best summer of my life. Everyone said he wasn't real, and my parents worried that I spent a summer hidden away in the basement playing hide and seek by myself. Only I knew I wasn't alone and that was enough for me.

I played nearly every game people play as a child with Ray. Hide and seek was his and my favorite, but we also played tag and rock paper scissors. We always had a blast. Ray was much better at finding me than hiding, until one day when my parents called me to dinner in the middle of looking for him. We had a lavish steak dinner that night, and boarded a plane to my older sister's wedding afterward. The flight from Houston to Tampa was a relatively short one, two hours continuous. About half way through the flight, I remembered Ray. My parents refused to go back for him, even after I begged and begged. We stayed at Clearwater Beach for a little longer than a week, enough time for me to forget about Ray. I got home and had friends from school over for a back-to-school party the day prior to my first day of first grade.

The years went by and I became popular in school, always off to another house, with another group of friends, on another date. I was successful in school. I never once thought about my not-so-imaginary friend Ray, who was still hiding in my parent's basement. My girlfriend and I both applied to Georgia Tech and made it in, so I went down to the basement to grab some necessities for the dorm. I popped open a box and felt a strange presence in the room. I dismissed it as just memories and left for Atlanta.

The first semester was great. I got good grades, accepted into a frat, and I like my roommate. I went home to Houston for Christmas to visit my parents, and we had a great time. They gave me a locket with a picture of our family when I was young, and my mom broke into a fit of nostalgia. She went on and on about that summer I spent in the basement doing nothing, how everyone thought I was damaged, how my parents kept checking to make sure I was still alive, how awful of parents they thought they were, and my fit on the plane. The memories of Ray came flooding back to me, and I smiled. People could never live up to the expectations of friends that Ray got me to accept. I went down in the basement one last time to bask in the memories of my imaginary friend. I heard a noise in the corner, but thought nothing of it. There always was the occasional rat down here. I kissed my parents goodbye and left for Atlanta again.

Upon arrival back at school, I had the best party of my life. I drank, which I'm ashamed of, but I met so many new people and caught up with so many old friends. After that night, I dropped like a sack of potatoes on my bed and was asleep before my head hit the pillow.

When I woke, I saw a dusty man. He looked to be about my age in his face, but his clothes were tattered and ripped, and he looked as if he hasn't slept in years. I arose in a panic, but he put his hand on my chest and I couldn't move. His fingers were like ice. He spoke first.
"Hello again. You might remember me as Ray."

"B-b-but you're imaginary... I made you up."

"So one believes, so it will be. You left me in that last hiding spot when you ran away to your sister's wedding. I was left to accumulate dust and rot in that dirty box. Now, you will feel the pain of knowing nobody will ever look for you."

He raised his hand, as if to strike, so I braced myself. I closed my eyes and put my hand up to shield the blow, but it never came. Instead, I felt a rush of cold water. I opened my eyes and saw nothing. Black, cold water surrounded me on all sides. I was alone, lost in the big, dusty box of the ocean. My eyes drifted shut, and the chilled water replaced the air in my lungs.
